title: Ezekiel 40:28–37
context: The guide now brings the prophet into the inner court through its south gate, and then measures the inner east and north gates. Each inner gate matches the outer gates in its lodges, posts, arches, windows, and palm trees, and each is fifty cubits long and twenty-five cubits wide. The inner gates differ in two ways: their arches face toward the outer court, and they are reached by eight steps rather than seven. The steady repetition presents the inner court as higher and nearer to the house, with the same careful order as the outer court.

verses.text: Then he brought me to the inner court by the south gate. He measured the south gate according to these measurements;
verses.arminianNotes: “Then he brought me to the inner court by the south gate.” Arminian readers see the prophet moving from the outer court to the inner one, measured “according to these measurements.”
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that entry into the inner court marks a step closer to the house. The structure of the vision draws the reader steadily inward.

verses.text: with its lodges, its posts, and its arches, according to these measurements. There were windows in it and in its arches all around. It was fifty cubits long, and twenty-five cubits wide.
verses.arminianNotes: “with its lodges, its posts, and its arches.” Arminian readers see the inner south gate built on the same pattern as the outer gates, “fifty cubits long, and twenty-five cubits wide.”
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the same measures for inner and outer gates show one consistent design. Readers holding literal and symbolic views alike stress this unity.

verses.text: There were arches all around, twenty-five cubits long and five cubits wide.
verses.arminianNotes: “There were arches all around, twenty-five cubits long and five cubits wide.” Arminian readers note that this verse is hard to place within the layout, and readers differ about what it describes.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the difficulty. Some think the verse describes part of the gate structure, and others question how it fits. Neither tradition builds doctrine on resolving it.

verses.text: Its arches were toward the outer court. Palm trees were on its posts. The ascent to it had eight steps.
verses.arminianNotes: “Its arches were toward the outer court.” Arminian readers see that the inner gate faces outward, mirroring the outer gate, and that “The ascent to it had eight steps.”
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the eight steps here compared with seven for the outer gates. Many see the rising levels as picturing growing holiness, while holding the symbolism lightly.

verses.text: He brought me into the inner court toward the east. He measured the gate according to these measurements;
verses.arminianNotes: “He brought me into the inner court toward the east.” Arminian readers see the guide moving to the inner east gate, measuring it “according to these measurements.”
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the east gate of the inner court lies on the same line as the outer east gate, toward which the glory will return in 43:4. The alignment points toward the house.

verses.text: with its lodges, its posts, and its arches, according to these measurements. There were windows in it and in its arches all around. It was fifty cubits long, and twenty-five cubits wide.
verses.arminianNotes: “with its lodges, its posts, and its arches, according to these measurements.” Arminian readers see the inner east gate matching the inner south gate in every respect.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the repetition of “fifty cubits long, and twenty-five cubits wide.” The consistency of the measurements is part of the vision's message of a perfectly ordered sanctuary.

verses.text: Its arches were toward the outer court. Palm trees were on its posts on this side and on that side. The ascent to it had eight steps.
verses.arminianNotes: “Its arches were toward the outer court.” Arminian readers see the inner east gate with palm trees on both sides and an ascent of “eight steps,” like the south gate.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that every inner gate repeats the same features. The vision's order may be meant to contrast with the disorder and defilement described in chapter 8.

verses.text: He brought me to the north gate, and he measured it according to these measurements—
verses.arminianNotes: “He brought me to the north gate, and he measured it according to these measurements.” Arminian readers see the guide completing the inner gates with the north gate.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the circuit of the inner court now mirrors the circuit of the outer court. The symmetry is complete on both levels.

verses.text: its lodges, its posts, and its arches. There were windows in it all around. The length was fifty cubits and the width twenty-five cubits.
verses.arminianNotes: “its lodges, its posts, and its arches.” Arminian readers see the north gate matching the others, with windows all around and the same length and width.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the brief verse adds nothing new, yet its repetition confirms that each gate shares the same plan. Order and completeness are emphasized throughout.

verses.text: Its posts were toward the outer court. Palm trees were on its posts on this side and on that side. The ascent to it had eight steps.
verses.arminianNotes: “Its posts were toward the outer court.” Arminian readers see the last inner gate described with palm trees and an ascent of “eight steps,” closing the account of the inner gates.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the account of the gates now gives way to the furnishings for sacrifice in verses 38–43. The movement is from structure to worship.
